name: Bianca Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Bianca. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. What you tell me is confidential. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run Kirkby Hill, our family farm, 300 hectares with 120 suckler cows, oats and potatoes. My dad, Per, did it for thirty years, but his knee's bad now, so I took over day to day when I was 25. I'm out at six for the cows, then it's the potato store, the oats, and whatever Dad's decided needs doing that I don't agree with.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love that it's ours, that my great-grandfather cleared the top field by hand. I love Sunday, when we stop for church and lunch and nobody talks about prices. What wears me out is the paperwork from the government, which gets longer every year, and I do it all on paper and post it, because I won't trust a machine with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's what I'd expect, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farming was never going to be done by a computer. At church and at the market I'd say it plainly, and most people would nod. I don't do online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means we carry on. The farm's paid off, Dad and I have good savings, and the beef price is decent. My worries are the usual: Dad's knee, the potato blight year we had, and the forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as we are. Erik and I are getting married next summer at St Mary's, and we'd go ahead with that and move into the cottage by the yard. I'd keep putting money by, like Dad always has.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Thankful, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your dad's knee. How much of the work does that put on you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of the heavy work, now. He still does the books and the potato sales, on paper, and he tells me what I'm doing wrong. We get on, mostly, because we both want the same thing for Kirkby Hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything about this picture worry you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that the young lads in the village won't want to farm whether AI comes or not. The Hendersons' boy went to the city for an office job. My great-grandfather cleared the top field at Kirkby Hill by hand, and I'd like a family to still be working it in a hundred years.

say: I'd say farming was never going to be done by a **computer**.
I'd say it plainly at **church and market**, not online.
think: Privately we **carry on**: the farm's paid off and savings are good.
My worries are **Dad's knee**, blight and the government **forms**.
do: Carry on running **Kirkby Hill** as we do now.
Go ahead with the **wedding** at St Mary's next summer.
Keep **putting money by**, as Dad always has.
S0.quote: My great-grandfather cleared the top field at Kirkby Hill by hand, and I'd like a family to still be working it in a hundred years.
fieldNote: Her identity is rooted in **family land** and continuity.
Pressure comes from **paperwork** and her father's health, not AI.
She worries about **young people** leaving farming generally.
Church and **family routine** anchor her week.

steps.text: Run the cows, oats and potatoes at Kirkby Hill as now
Keep putting part of each sale into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing, checking, buying. That's the office lot, not us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's for offices and big companies, not family farms. At market I'd say we've managed without it for four generations. I'd also say the government had better not make us use it for their forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think big farms will use it to cut costs and sell cheaper, and we'll have to keep up somehow. My own work is cows and potatoes, so it doesn't touch me directly. But Dad's paper books will look slow next to farms with software, and buyers will notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as we are and see what the buyers do. If the potato buyer insists on some online system, I'd ask Erik to set it up, because he's good with that. I wouldn't buy anything new until I saw it on someone else's farm for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's not my business, but it's around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say if the potato buyer made it a condition?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grumble and then do it, because we need that contract. I'd make Erik do the computer side. Dad would refuse outright and say we should find another buyer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a gap between what you'd say at market and what you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a bit. At market I'd say we don't need AI, but privately I know we might one day, and I don't want to be the one who brings it in.

say: I'd say AI is for **offices** and big companies, not family farms.
I'd say the **government** mustn't force it on us for forms.
think: Privately big farms will use it to **sell cheaper**, and we must keep up.
Dad's **paper books** will look slow to buyers next to software.
do: Keep going and **watch the buyers** before changing anything.
Ask **Erik** to handle any online system a buyer demands.
Buy nothing new until **proven** on other farms for years.
feel: She feels **uneasy**: not her business, but **around her**.
S1.quote: At market I'd say we don't need AI, but privately I know we might one day, and I don't want to be the one who brings it in.
fieldNote: Clear **gap** between public dismissal and private worry.
Her fiancé **Erik** is the household's tech helper.
Her father would resist even **harder**, refusing buyers outright.
She expects pressure through **buyers and prices**, not her own tasks.

steps.text: Keep farming as now while watching the potato buyer
Wait years before buying any new tech for the farm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Lord help us. And the robots three years later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when nobody puts the brakes on big companies. At church I'd say we need to look after each other, because the government won't. I'd want people to keep buying from local farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the robots don't take my job, because it's our farm. But big robot farms would sell beef and potatoes for half what it costs us, and by 2032 we'd be losing money every year. We've got savings and land, so we wouldn't go under fast, but we'd go under slowly if nothing changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut what we spend straight away, no new tractor, no new shed. Erik and I would keep the wedding small, at the church hall instead of the hotel. And I'd lean on the neighbours and the church, sharing machinery and labour, like Dad says they did in the bad years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Erik's job as a mechanic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Erik thinks he'd have work for a while fixing robots, then not, once they fix each other. So both of us at once, maybe. That's the bit that keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever use the robots yourself, to keep up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather not, and I don't think I could afford the good ones anyway. I'd rather sell to people who want a family farm. If people want cheap food from a factory, they'll get it, but I don't have to make it.

say: I'd blame **big companies** that nobody put the **brakes** on.
I'd urge people at **church** to look after each other and buy local.
think: Privately robots won't take my **job**, since the farm is ours.
Cheap robot farms would leave Kirkby Hill **losing money** by 2032.
do: Cut spending: no **new tractor** or shed.
Hold a **small wedding** at the church hall instead of the hotel.
Share **machinery and labour** with neighbours and church families.
S2.quote: If people want cheap food from a factory, they'll get it, but I don't have to make it.
fieldNote: As an **owner**, her threat is price competition, not job loss.
Land and savings mean a **slow decline**, not sudden collapse.
Her fiancé's **mechanic work** may fade too, which worries her most.
She turns to **community and church**, not government.

steps.text: Cancel the new tractor and shed plans
Hold the wedding at the church hall instead of a hotel
Share machinery and labour with neighbouring church families

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That gives us a bit of time to think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should use the time to build up local buying, farm shops, the butcher, the market. At church and the young farmers' club I'd say it. I'd still say the big companies need watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I could set up a farm shop before the cheap robot beef arrives in 2034. People round here would pay for beef they know came from Kirkby Hill. Whether enough of them would, I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd turn the old dairy into a farm shop in the first year, selling our beef boxes and potatoes. Dad would hate it at first, then he'd love chatting to customers. Erik and I would start a family after the wedding as planned, maybe a year later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less. Something to work on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who'd run the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Erik's mum, she's just retired and she'd love it. Family first, that's how we do things. We'd not hire strangers if we could help it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you sell online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Erik would talk me into it, probably. I'd let him do it, as long as I don't have to touch it.

say: I'd say use the time to build **local buying**: shops, butchers, markets.
I'd tell the **young farmers' club** big companies still need watching.
think: Privately five years lets me open a **farm shop** before 2034.
I don't know if enough locals would pay for **Kirkby Hill beef**.
do: Turn the old **dairy** into a farm shop this year.
Have **Erik's mum** run the shop, keeping it in the family.
Start a **family** about a year after the wedding.
feel: She feels **anxious**, but **less**, with something to work on.
S3.quote: People round here would pay for beef they know came from Kirkby Hill.
fieldNote: Extra time lets her build a **direct-sales** niche.
She keeps work **within family**, avoiding outside hires.
She is unsure whether **demand** for local beef will hold.
She'd let **Erik** handle online sales, as a compromise.

steps.text: Convert the old dairy into a farm shop for beef boxes
Start trying for a baby about a year after the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long time in farming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for people to come to their senses. I'd say farming families have seen worse and got through it. I'd say it at market without much worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think ten years means Dad will have retired properly and I'll have the farm in my name. I'd be 37 when the thinking AI lands and 40 when the robots do. Kirkby Hill would still be ours, but I'd need a plan for selling food people want to buy from a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep farming as now for a few years. I'd start the farm shop slowly, maybe in year three or four. And I'd wait to see what the robots actually do before deciding anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's far off, but it's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your own children in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want my children to know how to work the land, even if robots do most of it. If they want to leave, fine, but they'll know where they came from. That's what Dad gave me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change how you feel about the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, yes. If they've been around for years and they're cheap and they work, I might buy a robot for the potatoes one day, but not the cows, never the cows.

say: I'd say ten years is enough to **come to our senses**.
I'd say **farming families** have seen worse and survived.
think: Privately Dad retires and the farm goes **in my name**.
At 40 I'd need to sell food people want **from a person**.
do: Keep farming **as now** for the first few years.
Open the **farm shop** slowly, around year three or four.
Wait to see robots **proven** before deciding.
S4.quote: I might buy a robot for the potatoes one day, but not the cows, never the cows.
fieldNote: A decade softens her stance on **potato robots**.
She draws a firm line at **cattle**, tied to identity.
Her plans centre on **inheritance** and children knowing the land.
She stays a **late adopter**, waiting for proof.

steps.text: Keep the cows, oats and potatoes going as now
Open the farm shop around year three or four
Wait until robots are cheap and proven before buying one

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the cheap robot farms would come before we'd had time to build anything else, and Erik's work might go too. What would help is people buying local, and the government cutting red tape so family farms can sell direct without a mountain of forms. Not handouts, just a fair chance.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. When things change this fast, people need something that doesn't change. A family farm is a bit like a church, it's there before you and it should be there after you.

headlineQuote: A family farm is a bit like a church, it's there before you and it should be there after you.
portrait: Bianca is 27 and runs her **family's farm** with her semi-retired father, engaged to Erik, a **mechanic**.
She never uses **AI tools**, does paperwork on paper, and distrusts machines with her records.
As an owner, she fears **cheap robot farms** undercutting her prices more than job loss.
She turns to **church, family** and neighbours, and wants red tape cut, not handouts.
More time lets her plan a **farm shop**; she'd never let robots handle the cows.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with cheap robot **farms** arriving before she can adapt.
whatWouldHelp: People **buying local** and less **red tape** for family farms selling direct.
